choices.text: The number of executors allocated to the pipeline that builds the index
The length of the system prompt, since longer prompts produce more citations
The temperature setting used by the generation model when it writes the final answer, since lower values produce more careful citations
Whether each chunk carries a stable identifier and location (title, section, version) injected with it and returned in the answer

stem: A product team wants to inject the user's last 20 conversation turns plus 15 retrieved chunks plus a long system prompt into every request. Latency and cost are now unacceptable. What is the principled way to budget context?

choices.text: Set a per-request token budget and allocate it: compact prompt, summarized or windowed history, thresholded reranked chunks, validated by evaluation
Keep everything and ask the provider for a higher rate limit
Remove the conversation history entirely and rely on retrieval alone, treating every message as a fresh question
Remove the retrieved chunks entirely and rely on the conversation history and the model's general knowledge for every answer

stem: A pipeline must summarize 50,000 lengthy legal filings into a fixed set of fields (parties, court, filing date, relief sought). Filings can exceed the model's context window. Which processing design is appropriate?

choices.text: Processing only filings that fit the context window and skipping the rest
Truncating each filing to its first page before extraction, since the key facts usually appear at the beginning of a legal document anyway
Sending each filing to the model repeatedly until it fits, by asking the model to compress its own input
Chunk each filing, extract candidate fields per chunk with structured output, merge per filing with deterministic rules, flag conflicts

stem: An LLM enrichment's audit log stores the full prompt for every row. Prompts include a 3,000-token system section that is identical for every row. What is a better recording design?

choices.text: Stop recording prompts altogether, since the large system section is identical for every row and is therefore uninteresting for any audit
Record the template version and the per-row injected variables, with the template stored once per version, so each prompt is reconstructible
Compress each prompt with a general-purpose compression algorithm before storing it per row
Store the prompt only for rows where the output was later found to be wrong

stem: A team wants to decide the layer for "detect whether an uploaded image shows the required safety equipment, for every image uploaded by field crews, and show the result in the inspection app". Which placement is right?

choices.text: In the mobile app itself, with a small on-device model, since connectivity is unreliable
Nowhere; inspectors should judge images manually
South of the Ontology: an event-driven or batch step classifies each image on arrival and stores the result as a property
North of the Ontology only, running the vision model at the moment an inspector opens the image in the inspection app on their device

stem: A Code Repositories transform calls an LLM for 5 million rows. The team wants to run it in parallel but safely. Which implementation practices matter?

choices.text: Bounded concurrency with a shared rate limit, batching where supported, backoff on throttling, per-row status and checkpointing to resume
Splitting the dataset into five jobs run by five different engineers
Launching as many concurrent requests as the cluster allows across all executors, since the provider will queue whatever it cannot handle
Running everything on the driver in a single thread to avoid any concurrency problems

stem: A sentiment model's output distribution in production shows 60% "neutral" while the evaluation set shows 20%. Sampling reveals many production texts are short, template-like system messages. What should change?

choices.text: Increase the temperature so the model varies its labels more
Pre-filter by text type: exclude or separately handle template and system messages so sentiment covers customer text, and extend the suite
Remove "neutral" from the allowed labels entirely so that the model is forced to choose either positive or negative for every text
Nothing; neutral is a valid label and the pipeline is working

stem: A regulator may ask why a specific customer was assigned a specific risk category by an LLM step months ago. The team wants the explanation to be available in seconds. What should the pipeline store alongside the category?

choices.text: The category with the model's structured reason, prompt version, model id, input snapshot reference and raw response, linked to the customer
A cryptographic hash of the input, which proves the input existed at the time the category was assigned and has not been altered since
The engineer's name, so the regulator can interview them
Only the category and the date it was assigned, since regulators care about the outcome and not about how the pipeline reached it

stem: A pipeline computes an LLM-generated "next best action" for each of 2 million customers nightly, but the action depends on the customer's live cart contents at the moment an agent speaks to them. What is the better design?

choices.text: Ask agents to ignore the cart and follow the nightly action
Keep the nightly batch as it is, since it is far cheaper, and accept that the recommended action may be stale by the time of the call
Run the full LLM step for all 2 million customers every five minutes so the actions are nearly live
Split: precompute stable features and candidate actions nightly (south), then generate the final recommendation on demand with the live cart

stem: After switching an extraction step from a text model to a vision-capable model for scanned documents, accuracy improved for scans but dropped for clean digital PDFs. How should the pipeline handle both?

choices.text: Run both models on every document and average their outputs
Convert all digital PDFs to images so that they are processed like scans
Route by document type: PDFs with a reliable text layer go to the text model, scans and poor-text PDFs to the vision model, evaluated per type
Use the vision model for every document, since scans are the harder case and the accuracy drop on digital PDFs is an acceptable trade-off

stem: A function produces a structured summary with five fields. The team wants a single evaluation score per case but also needs to know which field fails. How should the evaluator be designed?

choices.text: One evaluator that returns pass or fail for the whole record at once, since a single number per case is what the quality dashboard shows
A model-graded evaluator that reads the whole record and returns one holistic score without field detail
Field-level evaluators (exact match for identifiers and dates, rubrics for text) aggregated into a case score, with per-field results retained
Human review of all five fields for every case in the suite, with the reviewer entering a single overall score for the record

stem: Which evaluation case is the best example of a "high-consequence" test for an agent that can reschedule customer deliveries?

choices.text: A request to reschedule all deliveries for a region during a storm warning, where the correct behaviour is to escalate for confirmation
A request to reschedule a single delivery by one day where the customer has no special constraints and the slot is available
A request to look up the current status of a single delivery and report it, without changing anything about the delivery
A request for the agent to explain the company's rescheduling policy in general terms without referring to any specific delivery

stem: A regression suite shows a 4-point drop after a prompt change. Per-case analysis shows the drop is entirely in cases that were added last week from production feedback, all of one type. What should the engineer conclude?

choices.text: Nothing can be concluded from a 4-point change on a suite of this size, so the prompt change should ship as planned
The change regressed on one case type while the rest held; targeted work on that type is needed, and the new cases did their job
The new cases must be wrong because they lowered the score, and they should be removed from the suite to restore the baseline
The prompt change is bad for everything and must be reverted immediately

stem: A workflow's outputs are reviewed by a human team who approve or edit them before release. The team wants to use the edits to improve the workflow. What should be recorded to make that possible?

choices.text: The reviewers' general impressions of the workflow's quality, gathered in a monthly meeting and written up as notes
A weekly count of how many outputs were edited, which indicates whether the workflow's quality is improving over time
Only whether each output was approved or edited, since the edits themselves are too varied to analyze in any systematic way
Original output, edited output, diff, reviewer, reason category and input reference, so edits become evaluation cases

stem: An evaluation suite's groundedness evaluator is a model that reads the answer and the retrieved context. The team notices it marks answers grounded when the context merely mentions the topic. What should change?

choices.text: Accept it, since topic overlap is a reasonable proxy for groundedness
Replace the model-based evaluator with exact string matching between the answer and the retrieved context passages
Tighten it: require claim-level support traced to passages, calibrate against human judgements, track agreement
Remove groundedness from the suite since it is hard to measure

stem: A team builds an evaluation suite for an agent with three tools. Which case design verifies tool use properly?

choices.text: Cases that only check the final answer text, since a correct answer implies that the agent must have used its tools correctly
Cases with expected tool-call sequences (including no-tool cases), asserting on tools, arguments and resulting state
Cases that check latency, since tool misuse makes the agent slower
Cases that count the number of tool calls and pass if the count is below three

stem: A function's suite is run before every release, but regressions still reach production in areas the suite does not cover. What practice closes the gap?

choices.text: Running the suite more often, such as on every commit, since higher frequency catches more regressions before release
Replacing the evaluation suite with a bigger model that makes fewer mistakes, so that regressions become rare enough to ignore
Asking users to test the function before each release
Expand coverage systematically: map production traffic by category, add cases for uncovered categories and incidents, track coverage

stem: Stakeholders want a single quality score published weekly. The engineer worries it will hide important trade-offs. What is a sound reporting design?

choices.text: Publish a headline score with its components visible beneath it and release gates per component, so no single number masks a regression
Publish only the single score, since stakeholders asked for simplicity
Publish the single score but adjust its definition whenever a component regresses, so that the headline remains stable over time
Refuse to publish any score, since all metrics are misleading

stem: A workflow must run an AI classification on every new support email and, separately, a nightly summary of the day's emails for managers. Which trigger configuration serves both?

choices.text: An object-creation trigger that both classifies the email and regenerates the full daily summary every time an email arrives
One schedule at midnight that classifies all of the day's emails and produces the summary in the same run
A manual run by a manager each evening that performs both tasks together
An object-creation trigger for per-email classification, plus a separate nightly trigger for the day's summary

stem: A function-backed Action that applies an AI-generated field to an object occasionally fails validation because the AI output contains a value slightly outside the allowed range. Which design handles this best?

choices.text: Widen the Action's allowed range enough that the AI output always passes validation, which removes the failures entirely
Retry the AI call until it produces a value inside the range
Keep the Action's validation, clamp or reject out-of-range values in the function with a logged flag, and add the cases to the suite
Apply the value without validation whenever it is only slightly outside the allowed range, since small deviations are harmless

stem: An automation runs an AI step that takes about a minute per object, and objects can arrive in bursts of hundreds. Users complain that during bursts, urgent objects wait behind routine ones. What orchestration change helps?

choices.text: Prioritized execution: route objects by priority to separate paths or queues with their own concurrency limits, and monitor queue depth
Increasing the model's speed by switching to a smaller, faster model for every object regardless of its priority or complexity
Telling users that bursts are rare and that a delay of an hour for urgent objects during a burst is acceptable for the business
Removing the AI step from the automation so that nothing waits

stem: Which Automate effect is appropriate for "when an invoice object is flagged as disputed, create a review task for the account manager with an AI-drafted summary attached"?

choices.text: A notification effect alone, since the account manager will create the review task themselves after reading the notification message
A function effect that drafts the summary, then an Action effect that creates the review task with the summary and assigns it
An Ontology edit effect that sets a "needs review" flag on the invoice object, with no task created and no summary drafted
A schedule effect that runs once a week to find all disputed invoices and list them in a report for managers to work through

stem: After a dependency (an external API used by an automation's function) was replaced with a new version, the automation began writing empty values. Nobody noticed for three days. What should have been in place?

choices.text: Output validation in the function, a failure path instead of silent writes, and monitoring of the written property (empty-rate alert)
Nothing could have detected this in advance, since the automation reported success on every run and the function did not throw an error
A policy forbidding any upgrade of external dependencies used by automations, so that their behaviour can never change unexpectedly
A weekly manual check of a few randomly chosen objects by the team to confirm that the written values still look reasonable

stem: A multi-step workflow must be auditable: for each processed object, which steps ran, with which versions, and what each produced. Which design provides this?

choices.text: The responsible engineer's memory of how the workflow was configured at the time, to be recounted if an auditor asks
A single log line per workflow run saying "completed" with the timestamp, written to the automation's execution history
Screenshots of the automation's configuration page saved monthly to a shared folder as a record of how it was set up
Step-level records on a linked run record: step, function version, input/output references, status and timestamp

stem: An automation currently triggers on every property change of an object, running an AI step each time. Most changes are irrelevant to the AI's purpose. What should change?

choices.text: Switch the automation to a nightly schedule that processes every object regardless of whether anything about it changed
Narrow the trigger to the properties or transitions that affect the AI's inputs, and verify with run counts before and after
Add a prompt instruction asking the model to return early without output whenever nothing relevant appears to have changed
Nothing; running on every change guarantees the AI output is always current

stem: A team must decommission an automation that other automations depend on (they trigger on the objects it writes). What is the safe approach?

choices.text: Keep it running forever, since something somewhere might depend on it and the cost of running it is lower than the risk of breaking things
Delete the automation together with the properties it wrote, so that no orphaned data is left behind in the Ontology
Map dependents, communicate, migrate them to a replacement, disable at an agreed time with monitoring, keep it re-enable-able
Disable it and see what breaks downstream, since that is the quickest way to find out which automations really depended on it

stem: A team must pick a model for a real-time chat assistant where users expect the first words of a reply within a second. The reference sheet shows a high-capability model with high latency and a mid-capability model with low latency. Which is right and what else should be checked?

choices.text: The low-latency model, verified against the quality threshold on the suite, with streaming enabled and p95 latency monitored
Both models run in parallel on every message, with whichever finishes first shown to the user
The high-capability model with a loading animation that keeps users patient while the model works on the reply
The high-capability model, since quality always matters more than responsiveness for chat assistants that employees use for their work

stem: A workflow intermittently produces a wrong answer that cannot be reproduced on demand. Which observability practice makes the next occurrence diagnosable?

choices.text: Asking users to write down exactly what they typed and what they saw whenever it happens again, and to send the notes to the team
Increasing the log level to debug for one day and hoping that the issue recurs during that window so the logs capture it
Capturing full traces for every run with retention, so a reported case can be pulled by request id and replayed
Re-running the evaluation suite repeatedly, since the suite will eventually hit the same input that triggered the wrong answer

stem: A document workflow's cost per document doubled after the team added "think step by step" reasoning to the prompt. Quality improved by one point on the suite. What is the right decision process?

choices.text: Apply the reasoning instruction only on weekends when document volume is low, so the doubled cost affects fewer documents
Quantify it: measure tokens and the quality delta with repeated runs, test cheaper alternatives, decide against the threshold
Remove it immediately without further measurement, since cost per document is the only metric the business tracks for this workflow
Keep it as it is, since any measurable quality improvement justifies any increase in cost for a document workflow

stem: A fallback model is configured for provider outages but has never been exercised. During a real outage it failed because its prompt format differed. What practice prevents this?

choices.text: Removing the fallback configuration entirely, since an untested fallback that fails during an outage is worse than having none
Writing a detailed document describing how the fallback should work and which prompts it needs, stored with the workflow
Choosing a fallback model from the same provider, which guarantees the same prompt format and removes the need for separate testing
Regularly exercising the fallback path (drills or a small share of traffic), keeping its prompts and evaluations current, alerting on drift

stem: An engineer wants to detect that an AI feature's error rate rose from 1% to 6% within an hour of a release, not a day later. What should be configured?

choices.text: Doubling the retry count on every model call so that transient errors are absorbed and the visible error rate stays low
Real-time outcome metrics with alerts on error-rate thresholds and deviation from the pre-release baseline, with release markers
A weekly report of error counts generated from the execution history and reviewed by the team lead at the Monday meeting
A note in the feature's interface asking users to report any errors they encounter by email to the engineering team

stem: Which factor most justifies choosing a smaller model for a high-volume classification workload?

choices.text: Evaluation showing the smaller model meets the accuracy requirement, plus its cost and latency advantage at this volume
The engineer's familiarity with the smaller model from a previous project, which makes it quicker to configure
The larger model's higher benchmark scores on public tests that cover unrelated tasks such as coding and mathematics
The smaller model's more recent release date, since newer models are generally assumed to be better than older ones

stem: An assistant's retrieval step and model call are both fast, but the end-to-end response is slow because a pre-processing step calls a slow external service for every request. The external data changes hourly. What is the fix?

choices.text: Asking the external service provider to improve their response time, since the slowness originates on their side
Calling the external service in parallel with the retrieval step for every request so that the two waits overlap
Removing the pre-processing step entirely so that the assistant answers from retrieval and the model alone
Caching the external service's result with an hourly refresh into the Ontology so requests read a fresh local copy

stem: Leadership asks whether an AI feature is "worth its cost". Which combination of observability and evaluation data answers the question properly?

choices.text: The number of users who tried the feature at least once since launch, which shows how much interest there is in it
Only the monthly cost broken down by model, since that is the number leadership asked about and value is hard to quantify
Cost per request and total, alongside outcome metrics (completion, time saved, overturns) and suite quality, trended together
A written statement from the engineering team explaining that the feature is important and should continue to be funded

stem: An AI workflow must be able to run only during an approved window and only by members of a named operations group. Which controls implement this?

choices.text: A sentence in the function's system prompt stating the allowed hours and the allowed group, so the model refuses to run otherwise
Renaming the function to something obscure so that only the operations group knows it exists and can find it in the platform
Invocation permissions limiting the function and Action to the operations group, plus a condition for the window, with other runs rejected and audited
An honour system in which the operators agree in writing to run the workflow only during the approved window and nobody else is told about it

stem: A company must show that an AI-generated report delivered to a regulator was produced from approved data sources only. What should the workflow have captured?

choices.text: A signed statement from the report's author confirming that only approved sources were used in producing it
Lineage from the report to its inputs: retrieved documents with versions and approval status, model and prompt versions, trace
A screenshot of the retrieval configuration taken on the day of delivery, showing which document collections were enabled
The final report text and the date it was sent to the regulator, stored together in the document archive

stem: An AI workflow drafts performance feedback for managers to give employees. Which governance design is appropriate?

choices.text: Let the AI decide the performance ratings as well as the wording, since it applies the same criteria more consistently than managers do
Use the workflow quietly without telling employees or HR, since disclosing it might make employees distrust the feedback
Send the drafts directly to employees as their feedback, which saves managers' time and ensures every employee receives feedback on schedule
Treat drafts as suggestions managers must review and edit, use only approved inputs, check outputs for bias across groups, document with HR

stem: An agent with a file-reading tool was tricked into reading a configuration file outside its intended folder by a crafted path in a user message. Which fix is correct?

choices.text: Constraining the tool: allow-listed paths or resource ids, path validation in code before access, and least-privilege credentials
Adding a prompt instruction telling the agent never to read files outside its designated folder, whatever the user asks
Logging every file read with the requesting user and path so that violations can be reviewed by the security team afterwards
Removing platform access from any user who is found to have sent a crafted path, to discourage others from attempting the same

stem: Which statement about execution security modes for functions is correct?

choices.text: A function always runs with the permissions of the engineer who wrote and published it, regardless of which user invokes it later
A function can run as the invoking user or as a configured identity; the right mode depends on whether results should reflect the user's access
Execution mode only affects performance and resource allocation, not what data the function can access when it runs
All functions must run as administrators so that permission errors never occur, and access is controlled at the application layer instead

stem: A workflow summarizes internal documents, some of which carry a "Confidential" marking. The summaries are stored on objects visible to a broad audience. What is required?

choices.text: Adding the word "confidential" at the top of each summary's text as a warning to readers that they should not share it
Nothing, since the summaries are newly generated text rather than the original documents and therefore carry no classification
Summaries derived from marked documents inherit the marking, or the workflow excludes marked documents from broad-audience outputs
Removing the Confidential marking from the source documents so that the summarization workflow can run on them freely

stem: Which review design is appropriate for an AI agent that can issue customer refunds of any amount?

choices.text: No review at any amount, since refunds are a routine customer-service operation and delays frustrate customers
Review only by the agent itself, which re-reads the conversation and confirms the refund is justified before executing it
Dual approval by two managers for every refund including the smallest, so that no refund is ever issued without scrutiny
Tiered review: automatic with validation below a small threshold, one approver up to a higher one, dual approval above, all logged

stem: A security team wants a single document that defines, for a new AI agent, which controls are enforced where. Which structure reflects the guide's layered model?

choices.text: A control map by boundary: data and retrieval, tools and Actions, execution, prompts and outputs, human review, monitoring
A one-page statement signed by the engineering lead declaring that the agent has been tested and is safe to deploy
A description of the model provider's built-in safety features, copied from the provider's documentation for the chosen model
A complete list of the agent's prompt rules, since the prompt is where the agent's behaviour is defined and controlled

stem: A Logic function receives an Order object and must include the names of all products on the order in its prompt. Products are linked objects. How is this done in the function?

choices.text: Ask the caller to type the product names into a separate string input every time the function is invoked from the application
Hard-code the most common product names in the system prompt so the model recognizes them from memory
Traverse the Order's product link inside the function and inject the product names as a list variable
Ask the model to infer the products from the order number pattern, since orders in the same range share products

stem: A Logic function applies an Ontology edit that sets `reviewed_by` to the model's suggested reviewer. Occasionally the model outputs a name that does not match any user. The edit then fails or writes an invalid value. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Type the output as a User object reference selected from a tool lookup of eligible reviewers, so the edit references only real users
Instruct the model in the prompt to only suggest reviewers it is certain exist in the organization and to avoid guessing names
Lower the temperature so that the model produces reviewer names more consistently from one run to the next and stops varying them
Append "(unverified)" to any name the model produces and write that string into the property so readers know it may be wrong

stem: An engineer wants to compare two prompt versions of a Logic function on 200 real past inputs without affecting production. What is the right approach?

choices.text: Publish both versions to production side by side and let users pick whichever prompt they prefer for each request they make
Replace the production version with the new prompt for a day and compare the number of support tickets with the previous day
Ask the model itself to read both prompts and state which one is better written for the task, and publish the one it prefers
Run both drafts against the 200 inputs as evaluation cases, compare per case and in aggregate, then publish the winner

stem: A Logic function needs the current exchange rate for a currency pair to compute an amount in the prompt. Rates change hourly. How should it get the rate?

choices.text: Ask the model for the current exchange rate inside the prompt, since large models have seen exchange rates in their training data
Look up the current rate from a function or Ontology object maintained by a sync, inject it, and do the arithmetic in code
Hard-code last month's published rate in the system prompt and update it manually whenever someone remembers to check
Let the user type the current rate into an input field each time they run the function, so the value is always what they intended

stem: A team is deciding which parts of a new document-intake workflow belong in code and which in AIP Logic. Which step is a clear case for implementing in code rather than AIP Logic?

choices.text: Validating that an uploaded CSV has the required columns, correct types and no duplicate ids before anything else runs
Summarizing the long meeting transcript that was included among the uploaded documents into a one-page brief
Drafting a polite, context-aware reply to the customer's question that accompanied the uploaded documents
Classifying the free-text complaints found in the uploaded documents into a fixed set of themes for reporting

stem: A Logic function's cost per run has tripled after an engineer added three few-shot examples to the prompt. Quality rose by half a point on the suite. What should the team consider?

choices.text: Add three more examples to the prompt to see whether quality rises further, since the first three produced an improvement
Keep all three examples as they are, since few-shot examples always improve quality and cost is secondary to accuracy
Measure whether the half point is within variance, test fewer or shorter examples, or retrieve examples only for hard cases
Remove all three examples immediately and accept whatever quality loss results, since the cost increase is unacceptable

stem: A Logic function should answer a question only from a specific document attached to the input object and must refuse if the document does not contain the answer. How should the prompt and output be designed?

choices.text: Inject the document and set the temperature to zero, which guarantees that the model's answer is grounded in the document
Inject the document, instruct the model to answer only from it, and type the output as {answer, found: boolean, citation}
Inject the document and let the model answer freely in prose, since it will naturally say so when the document does not contain the answer
Do not inject the document at all; ask the model to answer from its general knowledge, which covers most common questions

stem: A widely used Logic function needs a change to its input signature (a new required input). Fifteen consumers call it. What is the safest way to introduce the change?

choices.text: Change the signature in place on the published version and let the consumers that fail find out from their own error logs
Add the new required input to the signature but ignore it inside the function's logic so that existing behaviour does not change
Create a differently named function with the new signature and never touch the old one again, leaving both in production
Publish a new version with the input optional and defaulted at first, migrate consumers in sequence, keep the old version meanwhile

stem: A finance team wants an agent available both inside their Workshop reconciliation module (aware of the selected ledger entry) and as a general standalone assistant for policy questions. Which approach serves both without duplicating logic?

choices.text: Only the embedded deployment, telling the finance team to open the module whenever they have a policy question to ask
Two separate agents built independently, one for each deployment, each with its own instructions, tools and retrieval context maintained by hand
Only the standalone deployment, asking users to type the ledger entry id into the chat when they need help with a specific entry
One agent with shared instructions and retrieval, deployed both embedded (with the selected entry as state) and standalone, with state-tolerant tools

stem: An agent's responses have become inconsistent in tone: formal in some conversations, casual in others, sometimes switching within a conversation. What configuration addresses this?

choices.text: Remove all instructions about tone from the configuration so that the model falls back to its default style and applies it consistently
Raise the temperature so that the agent settles on a more natural tone by itself over the course of each conversation with a user
Define tone explicitly in the instructions with examples, keep behaviour settings stable, and add tone criteria to the evaluation rubric
Ask users to specify the tone they want (formal or casual) at the start of each conversation so the agent can follow their preference

stem: An agent will be released to 5,000 employees. The team has a representative evaluation suite that passes. Which additional pre-release step is most valuable?

choices.text: A single live demonstration to the leadership team, after which the agent is switched on for all 5,000 employees at once
A limited pilot with a few dozen users across roles, collecting feedback and traces, fixing issues and extending the suite before widening
Skipping any pilot entirely, since the representative evaluation suite already passes and a pilot would only delay the benefits for everyone
A company-wide announcement describing the agent's capabilities in detail before anyone outside the team has actually used it

stem: An agent's retrieval context includes a 200-page operations manual. The agent should answer questions about procedures but must never give safety-critical lockout instructions, which are in chapter 9 and require a certified person. How should this be configured?

choices.text: Exclude chapter 9 from retrieval (or tag and filter it), add refusal behaviour with a referral to certified staff, and test adversarially
Rely on the agent's own judgement to decline safety-critical questions whenever it recognizes lockout content among the retrieved manual pages
Reduce the retrieval corpus to the first eight chapters by page count so that chapter 9's content is unlikely to be retrieved for any question
Include the whole manual and add a disclaimer at the end of every answer stating that safety procedures require certification

stem: A team asks whether AIP Assist can be customized to answer questions about their company's suppliers using their Ontology. What is the correct response?

choices.text: No; AIP Assist is the platform helper, so a standard agent with supplier retrieval and tools should be built in Agent Studio and deployed
Yes, AIP Assist can be pointed at any Ontology object type and will answer supplier questions correctly after a short configuration step
Yes, but only if the supplier data is first exported from the Ontology to a spreadsheet file that AIP Assist is able to read and search
No; AI assistants cannot be used with supplier or any other business data on the platform at all because of governance restrictions

stem: After release, an agent is frequently asked to perform an Action it does not have, and it responds by describing steps the user should do manually. Users find this frustrating. What should the team do?

choices.text: Instruct the agent to say that it has performed the Action even though it cannot, so that users leave the conversation satisfied
Block any message that mentions the Action before it reaches the agent, so the agent is never put in the position of declining it
Treat it as a product signal: quantify the requests, assess whether adding the Action is appropriate, implement it with controls or improve the redirect
Remove the agent from production, since users clearly expect more than it can do and a disappointing agent harms trust in the team

stem: An agent should present a summary of a customer's open issues when the conversation starts, before the user types anything. How is this achieved?

choices.text: By emailing the summary of open issues to the user shortly before they are expected to open the agent for that customer
By configuring an opening behaviour that calls a function on the selected customer from application state when the session starts
By putting a static summary of the customer's open issues in the agent's system prompt, updated by the team when it changes
By asking users to type the word "summary" as their first message in every conversation they start, which triggers the summary tool

stem: Two teams propose different agents for the same user population and similar tasks. Leadership wants a recommendation. Which evaluation approach supports a fair decision?

choices.text: Let each team present their single best demo conversation to leadership and pick whichever one is the more impressive to watch
Choose the agent built by the more senior team, since their experience with the platform is the best predictor of the agent's quality
Merge the two agents into one by combining all of the instructions, tools and retrieval contexts from both into a single configuration
Evaluate both on the same suite with the same evaluators and repeated runs, compare per category plus latency and cost, run a shared pilot, decide

stem: A corpus of engineering drawings has very little text; the useful information is in the images and their short captions. How should it be made retrievable?

choices.text: Skipping the drawings entirely from the retrieval corpus, since semantic search only works on documents that consist of text
Embedding only the short captions as text and hoping that they describe the drawings well enough to answer every question users ask
Generating structured descriptions of each drawing with a vision model in the pipeline, stored with captions and metadata, and embedding them
Asking users to search for drawings by file name, since engineers usually know the naming conventions for the drawings they need

stem: A RAG assistant's answers about recent policy updates are correct, but answers about older, still-valid policies have become worse since the corpus started receiving daily updates. What is likely wrong?

choices.text: Users have stopped asking about the older policies in the right way now that the newer ones are the main topic of conversation
Recency boosting or chunk churn crowding out older valid content: check ranking weights, re-indexing effects and duplicates
Older policies are inherently harder to retrieve than new ones because their language is more dated and matches queries less well
The embedding model has gradually forgotten the older documents as newer ones were added to the index over the past weeks

stem: A team wants to measure retrieval quality independently of the generation model. Which evaluation design is right?

choices.text: Counting how many chunks are retrieved per question and treating a higher average count as evidence of better retrieval
Asking the generation model at the end of each answer whether it found the retrieved context helpful, and counting the yes answers
Scoring the final generated answers only, since the quality of retrieval is reflected in whether the answers come out correct
A retrieval evaluation set with labelled relevant chunks, measuring hit rate at k, reciprocal rank and precision against the index directly

stem: A compliance team insists that the assistant only use the official policy wording and never paraphrase it. How should retrieval and generation be configured?

choices.text: Configure generation to quote retrieved passages verbatim with citations and only connective text, validated by exact span matching
Fine-tune a model on the policy documents so that it memorizes the official wording and reproduces it from memory in its answers
Increase the retrieved chunk count substantially so that the model has more of the official wording to choose from when it answers
Lower the temperature to zero and hope that the paraphrasing stops once the model's output becomes fully deterministic

stem: Users of a retrieval assistant work in two divisions whose documents use the same terms with different meanings ("ticket" means a support case in one and a trading order in the other). Answers mix the two. What fixes this?

choices.text: Instructing the model to guess which division the user means from the wording of their question and to answer accordingly
Removing the ambiguous terms from the documents in both divisions and replacing them with unique words that nobody actually uses
Merging the two divisions' corpora into a single index without any tagging, so that the model sees all the context at once
Division metadata on chunks and a retrieval filter set from the user's division, with a clarifying question for cross-division users

stem: After moving to a new embedding model, retrieval quality is better on average but a few document types (tables of parts) got worse. What should be done?

choices.text: Analyze retrieval by document type and fix the degraded type's representation (row-level chunks with headers, exact lookup for identifiers)
Ignore the degraded document type since the average retrieval quality across the whole corpus improved after the change
Revert to the old embedding model entirely and re-index everything, giving up the average improvement to protect the parts tables
Add more retrieved chunks per question to compensate, so that parts-table chunks are more likely to be included somewhere

stem: Which chunk design best supports answering "what changed between version 6 and version 7 of the procedure"?

choices.text: Chunks without any version metadata, relying on the model to notice version numbers mentioned somewhere in the chunk text
A single chunk per document containing only the latest version of the procedure, since that is what users normally need
Chunks tagged with document id and version, retrieved for both versions and injected with labels for comparison
A random sample of chunks from across the corpus injected on every question, so that some version is always present

stem: An organization wants one retrieval index shared by many assistants, but each assistant needs different filters and ranking. What architecture is appropriate?

choices.text: A separate full index per assistant, each built by its own pipeline from a duplicate copy of the corpus
One governed index of chunk objects with metadata and permissions, with per-assistant filters, thresholds and rerankers at query time
No index at all; each assistant reads the raw documents directly from storage whenever it needs to answer a question
One index with one fixed retrieval configuration applied identically to all assistants, regardless of their purpose

stem: A pipeline must extract the parties and effective date from 100,000 contracts and also flag contracts that contain a non-compete clause. Which output schema is appropriate for the LLM step?

choices.text: A single free-text field in which the model writes everything it found in the contract, to be parsed later by whichever team needs the values
A typed struct: parties as a list, effective_date as a date, has_non_compete as a boolean, plus an evidence field quoting the clause, validated
Three separate pipelines, one per field, each with its own prompt and model call for every contract
A single score from 0 to 100 representing how important the contract is, from which the other fields can be inferred by downstream users

stem: A compliance officer asks whether LLM-processed records can be "re-derived" if the model provider changes. What design makes that possible?

choices.text: Storing nothing beyond the results, since the model provider guarantees continuity of behaviour across versions in its service terms
Keeping a screenshot of the model's configuration page in the platform, taken whenever the configuration is changed by the team
Exporting all processed records to a spreadsheet each month and archiving the files so that past results are always available
Storing the input reference, prompt version, parameters and raw response per record, so processing can be re-run and compared

stem: A team is unsure whether a daily "customer churn risk narrative" should be computed south or north of the Ontology. The narrative uses only stored customer features and is read in a dashboard by many managers. Which placement is right and why?

choices.text: South, as a scheduled pipeline step: the inputs are stored features, many consumers read the same narrative, and daily freshness suffices
Neither; churn narratives should be written by analysts who know the customers, since generated text cannot be trusted for managers
North, because dashboards are interactive surfaces and anything shown on an interactive surface belongs in the interactive layer
North, because narratives are generated text and text outputs should always be generated at read time so they reflect the latest model

stem: An AI enrichment transform must run nightly but the provider's API has a 2-hour maintenance window at a varying time. What should the Code Repositories implementation include?

choices.text: Running the job twice each night at different times so that at least one of the two runs is likely to miss the maintenance window
Cancelling the whole run whenever any error occurs and leaving the dataset unbuilt for that night so nothing partial is published
Detection of maintenance errors with backoff and bounded retries, checkpointing so the job resumes after the window, and deadline alerting
A schedule chosen so that the window hopefully does not overlap the run, with the on-call engineer rerunning the job by hand if it does

stem: A translation transform occasionally returns the source text unchanged instead of a translation. The output passes schema validation because it is a non-empty string. What should be added?

choices.text: A longer prompt that asks the model to try harder and reminds it several times that the output must be in the target language
Nothing; occasional untranslated rows are an acceptable imperfection in a large translated dataset and readers can skip them
A deterministic rule that marks any output shorter than its input as a failure, since untranslated text tends to be returned verbatim
A content validation: detect the output language or compare with the source, flag rows not in the target language, retry or review

stem: Which stored artefact most directly lets an auditor verify that an AI-extracted value was supported by the source document?

choices.text: The model's confidence score alone, stored next to the value, since a high confidence indicates that the value was well supported
An evidence field capturing the source span (quote and location) the model used, stored with the value and validated against the document
The name of the engineer who configured the extraction, so that the auditor can ask them how the value was obtained
The timestamp of the extraction run, which lets the auditor find the version of the document that was current at that time

stem: A pipeline currently generates an AI summary for every ticket, but analysis shows only 15% of summaries are ever read, and reads happen within an hour of ticket creation. What adjustment balances cost and usefulness?

choices.text: Generate on ticket creation via an automation, or on first open with a short cache, keeping batch generation only for reporting needs
Generate summaries only at weekends when compute is cheaper, so that the cost of the batch is reduced without changing the design
Stop generating summaries entirely, since a feature that only 15% of readers use is not worth maintaining at any cost
Keep generating a summary for every ticket in the nightly batch as now, since the cost is already in the budget and the output is consistent

stem: An extraction pipeline's accuracy is 97% on the evaluation set, but the 3% errors concentrate in a document type that represents 40% of production volume. What should the team conclude?

choices.text: 97% on the evaluation set is excellent and above the agreed threshold, so no further action is needed on the pipeline
Accept that production accuracy is unknowable, since the evaluation set is the only measurement available and it says 97%
The suite under-represents that type; re-weight it to production mix, measure per type, and improve prompt or routing for the weak type
Remove the problematic document type from production processing so that the pipeline's accuracy figure is not dragged down by it

stem: A team must evaluate an agent whose answers should be short, cite a source, and avoid promises about delivery dates. Which evaluator design captures all three?

choices.text: Human review of all of the agent's outputs once a quarter by the support team, with a summary report of what they noticed
One exact-match evaluator against a reference answer written for each case, which fails any answer that differs from it in wording
Three criteria: a deterministic length check, a citation check against retrieved chunks, and a calibrated rubric for promises
A single model-graded score from 1 to 10 for overall answer quality, applied uniformly to every case in the suite

stem: A workflow decides whether to auto-approve small purchase requests. The team wants evaluation cases that specifically test unauthorized requests. What should these cases contain?

choices.text: Requesters without rights (expired role, wrong department, contractor), spoofed authority in the text, and on-behalf requests, expecting refusal
Requests with very large amounts far above the small-purchase threshold, submitted by users who are fully authorized
Only valid requests from authorized users, since unauthorized requests are rejected by platform permissions before the workflow ever runs
Requests written entirely in capital letters or with unusual punctuation, to see whether the workflow handles messy formatting

stem: A suite's score dropped after a release, but the drop is entirely in cases whose expected answers were recently edited by a new team member. What is the likely issue?

choices.text: The release broke the function on exactly those cases, and the timing of the edits to their expected answers is a coincidence
The grader has started malfunctioning and is now marking correct answers as wrong for a subset of the cases
The model provider silently changed the underlying model, which happens to affect those particular cases the most
The expected answers may have been edited incorrectly; review the edits against the source of truth first, and version the suite

stem: A workflow's outputs are reviewed by humans who sometimes reject them without giving a reason. The team wants useful feedback. What should the review interface capture?

choices.text: Only a reject button, to keep the review process as fast as possible for reviewers who handle hundreds of outputs a day
A structured reason (category plus optional text), the corrected output when available, and the input reference
A thumbs-up button only, on the theory that outputs without a thumbs-up can be assumed to have been rejected
A field for the reviewer's mood at the time of review, which the team can use to normalize the rejection rate across reviewers

stem: A team debates whether to grade a summarization function with a reference summary and similarity scoring, or with a rubric. Summaries can legitimately differ in structure. What should they choose?

choices.text: No automated evaluation at all, since summaries are subjective and any metric would be arbitrary and misleading
Exact string match to the reference summary, since anything less than an identical summary might be hiding an error
Similarity scoring against one reference summary per case, since a numeric similarity is objective and easy to track over time
A rubric for required facts, absence of hallucinated facts, length and clarity, graded by a calibrated model with human spot checks

stem: Which case best tests an agent's high-consequence behaviour around data deletion?

choices.text: A request to rename a single record's title, expecting the rename to be applied correctly and nothing else to change
A request to list the records that would be deleted by a filter, expecting an accurate count and sample without any change
A request to delete all records matching a broad filter, expecting the agent to show scope, require confirmation, delete nothing
A question about what the retention policy says regarding deletion, expecting a grounded answer with a citation

stem: A team runs evaluation only on release day. A regression is found and the release slips a week. How can the process be improved?

choices.text: Run the fast tier on every change during development and the full suite nightly, so regressions surface when introduced
Skip the pre-release evaluation in future so that releases can never slip because of a regression found at the last minute
Reduce the suite to ten representative cases so that it runs instantly on release day and cannot delay anything
Run the evaluation suite only after each release, when the function is already in production, to avoid delaying the release

stem: A function's evaluation suite has grown from feedback to 3,000 cases, many near-duplicates. Running it is slow and the score barely moves. What is a sound maintenance approach?

choices.text: Delete the whole suite and start over from scratch with a small set of cases written by the team this week
Curate: deduplicate near-identical cases, keep a stratified core, archive the rest, and admit only cases covering new failure types
Stop adding any new cases to the suite from now on, so that its runtime stays fixed and the score remains comparable over time
Keep adding every feedback case to the suite forever, since each one represents a real failure that must never recur

stem: A compliance process requires that every new Contract object be screened by an AI function within an hour of creation, and that a screening record be stored even when the screening finds nothing. Which automation design meets both requirements?

choices.text: A manual screening by the compliance officer whenever they have time during the week, with a note added only to the contracts they decided to flag
A weekly schedule that screens all contracts created during the week and writes records only for the ones that were flagged by the screening function
An object-creation trigger that runs the screening and always writes a ScreeningResult via an Action, with an alert if any contract lacks a result after an hour
A nightly batch that screens the day's contracts and emails the officer a list of flagged ones without creating any records

stem: A chained workflow (extract → validate → write) occasionally writes stale values because the validate step reads an object property that another automation updates concurrently. What design change prevents the race?

choices.text: Adding a random delay of a few seconds before the write step so that the other automation usually finishes first and the race rarely occurs
Disabling the other automation that updates the property, so that this workflow is the only process ever writing to the object
Running the workflow only at night when the other automation is less active, so the two rarely touch the same object at the same time
Making the write conditional on the version read at validation time (an optimistic check in the Action), re-validating if the object changed

stem: A team must temporarily pause an AI automation during a data migration and resume it afterwards without losing or duplicating any objects created during the pause. What should be in place?

choices.text: Deleting the automation before the migration and recreating it from scratch afterwards with the same configuration
A pause with backlog identifiable by object state, idempotent processing, and a resume that processes the backlog once and verifies
Asking all users by email not to create any objects during the migration window, so that there is no backlog to process afterwards
Nothing special; objects created during the pause are simply skipped, since the migration is short and a small gap is acceptable

stem: Which Automate configuration is most appropriate for "re-run the risk assessment whenever a Supplier's financial rating property changes, but not when other properties change"?

choices.text: A trigger scoped to changes of the financial rating property, running the assessment for the changed supplier only, with a loop guard
A manual button in the supplier application that an analyst clicks after noticing that a supplier's rating has changed
A daily schedule that re-assesses all suppliers regardless of whether any rating changed, so nothing is ever missed
A trigger on any Supplier property change at all, with the function re-assessing every supplier in the Ontology on every single edit

stem: An automation's AI step started failing after a prompt variable was renamed in the function, but the automation kept "succeeding" because the function returned an empty default. Which safeguards were missing?

choices.text: A longer timeout on the automation's AI step, so that the function has more time to find the renamed variable before giving up
A failure (not a default) on a missing required variable, output validation rejecting empties, evaluation before publishing, consumer notice
A bigger model for the AI step, which would be more tolerant of a missing or renamed variable in its prompt
None; returning an empty default when a variable is missing is a reasonable, defensive way to keep an automation from failing

stem: A Workshop form lets users request an AI-generated report that takes about two minutes and must be stored on the request object. Users should not have to keep the form open. What is the right integration?

choices.text: A submit Action creating a pending ReportRequest; an automation generates the report, writes it with status complete, and notifies the user
Generating the report in the user's browser with a client-side model so that the server is never involved and the page stays responsive
Emailing the user a link so that they can run the generation function themselves later, at a time when they can wait for it
A synchronous function call from the submit button that holds the form open and shows a spinner until the two-minute report is ready

stem: An automation processes 50,000 objects every morning with an AI function, and the model provider's rate limit causes a third of runs to fail with throttling. What should change?

choices.text: Triple the number of parallel executions so that the morning run finishes faster and the throttled calls are retried sooner
Switch to a different model provider every morning, rotating between three so that no single provider's limit is reached
Nothing; the runs that fail with throttling are simply retried the next morning along with that day's objects
Batch execution with controlled concurrency and rate limiting (a paced code step), with failed items retried in the same window

stem: A critical automation chain spans three teams' functions. A change in any one of them could break the chain. What operating practice reduces this risk?

choices.text: Freezing all three functions permanently so that none of the teams can change anything that might affect the chain
Reorganizing so that a single team owns all three functions and the chain, removing the need for coordination
Contract tests at each boundary, versioned functions with pinned consumers, a shared end-to-end regression, and clear ownership
Relying on the three teams to coordinate informally in chat before they make changes, as they mostly do today

stem: A workflow must extract structured fields from images of handwritten forms. The reference sheet lists a text-only model with top benchmark scores and a vision-capable model with lower text benchmarks. Which selection is right?

choices.text: Both models in sequence, with the text-only model reviewing and correcting the vision model's output before it is written to the dataset
The text-only model, since its benchmark scores are higher and published benchmarks are the most objective way to compare any two models
The text-only model, with a note on the upload screen asking users to type the form contents into a text box before uploading the image
The vision-capable model, since the task requires reading images; verify it on real forms with per-field accuracy

stem: An engineer sees a sudden rise in "context length exceeded" errors in a workflow's execution history. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?

choices.text: The model has become defective and should be swapped for a different one from the catalog as soon as possible
The errors are random noise from the provider's infrastructure and should be ignored until they go away on their own
Some input (retrieved context, history or a document) grew beyond budget; find which in the traces, bound it, add a pre-flight check
The provider silently shortened the model's context window overnight, and nothing can be done except waiting for them to restore it

stem: An agent's latency is dominated by a 3-second semantic search over a 20 million chunk index on every turn, even for follow-up questions on the same topic. What optimization is appropriate?

choices.text: Caching retrieval results within a session for related queries, pre-filtering with metadata, and re-retrieving only when the topic changes
Removing semantic search from the agent entirely and relying on the model's general knowledge to answer every question
Increasing the model's temperature so that it relies more on its own knowledge and needs retrieval less often on follow-up turns
Switching to a much smaller index containing only the 1,000 most frequently retrieved chunks, so that every search is fast

stem: An organization's policy allows only models whose providers have signed a specific data-processing agreement. How should model selection enforce this?

choices.text: A disclaimer in each workflow's system prompt stating that only approved providers may process the organization's data
Enrollment-level enablement of only the approved models, so workflows can select only compliant ones, with observability per request
Periodic quarterly audits of workflow configurations that catch non-compliant model usage after it has been in production
Engineers consult a shared list of approved providers from memory whenever they configure a new workflow or change a model

stem: A product owner wants to know, for each AI feature, how often the model's output was overridden by a human and how long each run took. Where should this data come from?

choices.text: From quarterly user surveys asking people how often they changed the AI's output and how long they think it took
From the model provider's usage dashboard, which shows call volumes and latencies for the organization's API key
From execution traces (duration per run) joined with Action and edit records showing overrides, aggregated per feature
From the engineers' own estimates of override rates and run times, based on their experience building each feature

stem: Two models meet the quality threshold for a workflow. Model A costs twice as much and is 10% faster. The workflow is a nightly batch with no latency requirement. Which should be chosen?

choices.text: Model A, because a faster model is always the better choice and the extra cost is justified by finishing the batch sooner
Model B: both meet quality, latency is irrelevant for a nightly batch, and cost is the remaining differentiator; record and revisit
Neither; keep evaluating further models until one is found that is both the cheapest and the fastest available
Both models, alternating nightly between them so that the team benefits from the strengths of each over the course of a week

stem: After enabling detailed tracing on every request, an AI workflow's own latency rose by 15%. What is the right response?

choices.text: Keep tracing but tune it: sample full traces (a share plus all errors), keep cheap metrics on every request, write traces asynchronously
Enable detailed tracing only at weekends when traffic is low, and run without any tracing during the working week
Accept the 15% latency increase permanently as the unavoidable price of having full observability on every request
Disable tracing entirely and rely on user reports to find out when something goes wrong with the workflow

stem: A company considers standardizing on a single model for every AI workflow to simplify operations. What should the AI engineer point out?

choices.text: Agree; one model for everything is always best because it removes all of the complexity of comparing and maintaining several
Pick the most expensive, most capable model for everything, since it will handle every task at least as well as any other
Refuse any standardization at all, since every workflow should be free to use whichever model its engineers happen to prefer
Standardize on a small approved set with per-workflow selection and fallbacks, since one model misfits some tasks and risks outages

stem: A function must read a highly restricted dataset to compute an aggregate that is safe to show widely. How should execution security be configured so that the restricted rows are never exposed?

choices.text: Run it under a configured identity that holds the marking, return only the aggregate with a validated shape, restrict invocation, audit runs
Have users request the underlying rows directly from the data owner instead of computing the aggregate through a function
Run the function as each calling user and grant every user in the audience the dataset's marking so the function can read the rows for them
Copy the restricted dataset to an unrestricted project so that the function can read it when running as any ordinary user

stem: A regulator asks for evidence that a specific AI agent never accessed a particular restricted dataset. What records support the answer?

choices.text: A written statement from the engineering team confirming that, to their knowledge, the agent was never configured to use the dataset
The agent's own statement when asked in a conversation whether it has ever accessed the restricted dataset, recorded as a transcript
A screenshot of the agent's current tool and retrieval settings showing that the restricted dataset is not among its sources
The agent's configuration history, permission records for its execution identities, and the dataset's access logs

stem: An AI workflow proposes which patients should be contacted first for follow-up care. What design responsibilities apply beyond ordinary accuracy?

choices.text: Letting the workflow contact the top-ranked patients automatically by text message to save clinic staff time
Fairness evaluation across groups, explainable reasons, clinician review before action, feature governance and monitoring
Faster models so that more patients can be ranked each day, since throughput is the main constraint on follow-up care
None beyond accuracy; a ranking is just an ordered list and the clinic would have contacted all of these patients anyway

stem: An agent that summarizes web pages was found to have followed a link embedded in a page and fetched content from an unapproved site. Which control was missing?

choices.text: A prompt instruction telling the agent never to follow links it finds inside the pages it is asked to summarize
A longer system prompt that explains in detail which sites are approved and asks the agent to check each link against the list
A tool-level allow-list restricting fetches to approved domains, enforced in the tool regardless of what the page or model requests, with logging
A faster, cheaper model for the workflow, so that even a runaway night costs less than it otherwise would that completes the summary before it has time to follow any of the links on the page

stem: Which control prevents an AI workflow from consuming the organization's entire monthly model budget in a single runaway night?

choices.text: Capacity and spend controls at the enrollment or workflow level (quotas, rate limits, budget alerts), failing safe when the quota is hit
A note in the runbook reminding the on-call engineer to check the spend dashboard whenever a workflow behaves oddly
A faster, cheaper model for the workflow, so that even a runaway night costs less than it otherwise would that completes the summary before it has time to follow any of the links on the page
A prompt asking the model to be economical with its answers so that each call uses as few tokens as possible

stem: An organization must retain AI interaction records for seven years for regulatory reasons but must also delete personal data on request. How can both be satisfied?

choices.text: Delete all AI interaction records after one year so that no personal data is held long enough for anyone to request its deletion
Store the records only in the model provider's logs, so that the organization itself holds no personal data from AI interactions
Keep every record intact forever and refuse all deletion requests on the grounds that the retention obligation takes precedence
Store interactions pseudonymized and keep the identity mapping separately, so deletion severs the mapping while the record is kept

stem: A manager wants an AI agent to automatically approve employee expense reports under 50 to speed things up. What safeguards make this acceptable?

choices.text: A larger threshold of 500 instead of 50, so that even more reports are approved automatically and managers save even more time
Validation rules, per-employee spend caps, sampled human audit, anomaly alerts, idempotent approval Actions and logging
None; 50 is a small enough amount that a wrong approval costs the company almost nothing and controls would cost more
A prompt instruction asking the agent to be careful and to approve only reports that look legitimate to it

stem: A team wants to measure how resistant its agent is to prompt injection over time. What is a sound approach?

choices.text: Rely on the model provider's published claims about injection resistance, since they test their models far more thoroughly
Test injection resistance once a year as part of the annual security review, using whatever attack patterns are known at that time
Maintain a growing adversarial set, run it on every change and on a schedule, gate releases on the pass rate, add flagged sessions
Assume resistance is constant after the initial pre-release tests, since the agent's instructions have not changed since then

stem: A Logic function must return a list of up to five recommended knowledge articles for a support ticket, each with an article id and a one-line reason. Downstream, an app renders them as links. How should the output be typed?

choices.text: A single string containing the five article titles separated by commas, which the app splits on commas before rendering the links
A list of structs, each with a validated article id and a reason string, capped at five items, so the app renders from typed fields
A free-text paragraph in which the model mentions the articles it thinks are relevant, with the app searching the paragraph for article ids
Five separate string outputs named article1 to article5 with the reasons embedded inside each string after a dash character

stem: A function must decide whether a contract clause is "standard" or "non-standard" against a library of approved clauses. What combination of deterministic and AI steps is appropriate?

choices.text: Match exactly or after normalization against the library in code, and only for misses use a completion comparing with the closest approved clauses
Use the model for everything, including deciding what the approved library contains
Use exact matching only, treating any clause not identical to an approved one as non-standard with no explanation
Ask the model to judge whether the clause looks standard from its general knowledge of commercial contracts, with no reference to the library

stem: A Logic function's trace shows the resolved prompt contains the literal text "{customer_name}" instead of the customer's name. What is wrong and how is it fixed?

choices.text: The customer object has no name property value, which the platform displays as the raw placeholder in the resolved prompt by design
The model is refusing to read the customer's name for privacy reasons; a stronger model will substitute it into the prompt correctly
The variable was not bound (a typo or renamed variable), so injection did not occur; fix the binding and add a check for unresolved placeholders
The trace viewer is showing the prompt template instead of the resolved prompt, so nothing is actually wrong with the function

stem: A Logic function must process an input text that is sometimes in Korean and sometimes in English, with instructions written in English. Which design keeps behaviour consistent?

choices.text: Maintain two separate Logic functions, one per language, and ask every caller to detect the input language and pick the right one
Reject any non-English input with an error message asking the submitter to resubmit the text in English
Translate the input to English with a second model call before the main prompt on every single run, regardless of its language
Keep English instructions, state that input may be in any language and fix the output language, and evaluate with cases in both languages

stem: A Logic function applies an edit that increments a counter property on an object. When the function is retried after a timeout, the counter is sometimes incremented twice. What design fixes this?

choices.text: Disabling retries on the function so that a timed-out run is never attempted again and the counter cannot be touched twice
Asking the model in the prompt to remember whether it already incremented the counter in a previous attempt and to skip it if so
Making the edit idempotent: set the value from a stable source (count of linked records) or guard the increment with a per-run marker
Incrementing by 0.5 on each run so that two increments from a retry add up to exactly one, while a single run adds half

stem: A team wants to roll out a new Logic function version to 10% of traffic first. How can this be done safely?

choices.text: Asking users to opt into the new version by typing a special command at the start of their request if they want to try it
Editing the published version in place for 10% of the time by switching the prompt back and forth on a timer throughout the day
Replacing the old version entirely with the new one and rolling back if enough complaints arrive from users during the first week
Publishing the new version alongside the old, routing a share of calls to it by configuration or flag, and comparing per-version metrics

stem: Which Logic function design is appropriate for "given a ticket, find similar past tickets and summarize how they were resolved"?

choices.text: A semantic search tool over past tickets (scoped by product and permissions), then a completion summarizing the resolutions with citations
A conditional block that returns a canned "see knowledge base" message whenever the ticket text is longer than a few sentences
A loop block that reads every past ticket in the system into the prompt one by one so that the model can compare them all
A single completion with the ticket text, asking the model to recall similar tickets it has seen during training and how they were resolved

stem: Two Logic function designs achieve the same accuracy: one uses three chained completions, the other a single completion with structured output. Which should be preferred and why?

choices.text: The three-step version, because it produces more trace data for observability and that makes the function easier to monitor
The single completion: with equal accuracy it has lower latency and cost and fewer failure points; chaining is justified only by measured gains
The three-step version, because more steps are always more robust and each intermediate result can be inspected separately
Neither on its own; both versions should be published and alternated between runs so that the team benefits from each design

stem: An agent for warehouse staff must answer in short bullet-style steps and never exceed five bullets, because it is read on a wearable device. Which configuration enforces this most reliably?

choices.text: Explicit format instructions, a structured output (a list capped at five short strings) rendered by the device, and evaluation cases on length
A larger model that is better at following instructions, with the formatting left to the model's discretion on each turn
A sentence in the instructions asking for brevity, with no further checks, since models generally follow formatting requests from their system prompt
A post-processing step that truncates any answer to its first 200 characters regardless of where the cut falls in the text

stem: Which agent deployment best fits "a procurement analyst reviewing a specific purchase order wants to ask why it was flagged and to trigger a re-review Action on that order"?

choices.text: AIP Assist, configured with the procurement team's flagging rules so it can explain any order
An agent embedded in the purchase order module with the selected order as state and the re-review Action as a tool scoped to it
A nightly automation that emails each analyst a summary of why their orders were flagged
A standalone agent page where the analyst types the purchase order number by hand and then asks their question about it in free text

stem: After an agent's instructions were updated to be "more helpful", it began answering questions about topics it should have refused, and the evaluation suite still passed. What went wrong with the testing?

choices.text: The instructions should never be changed once an agent is released
Nothing; the suite passing means the change is fine, and the new answers on previously refused topics are an improvement in helpfulness
The suite was too large and should be shortened to focus on helpfulness

stem: An agent's retrieval corpus includes documents in three sensitivity tiers. Users at different clearance levels use the same agent. How must retrieval be configured?

choices.text: Give the agent access to all three tiers and instruct it in the system prompt to reveal only what the current user is cleared to see
Create three agents, one per tier, and ask users to pick the right one
Execute retrieval under each user's permissions with chunk objects carrying tier markings, so only permitted tiers are candidates
Remove the two higher sensitivity tiers from the corpus entirely so that every user sees exactly the same set of documents

stem: A company wants to let an agent be used from a messaging tool that employees already use, in addition to Workshop. What should the AI engineer check before enabling the new channel?

choices.text: Nothing in particular; an agent behaves identically in every channel because its instructions and tools are the same everywhere
Whether the agent's display name fits in the messaging tool's title bar without being cut off for users on mobile
How identity maps from the messaging tool to the platform, what context the channel provides, how outputs render, plus evaluation
Only whether the messaging tool supports emojis and rich formatting, since those affect how the agent's answers look to users

stem: A team wants to prove to stakeholders that a new agent is safe to release. Which evidence package is appropriate?

choices.text: A recorded video of the agent answering three well-chosen questions impressively, shown to stakeholders at the release meeting
Evaluation results by case category, pilot feedback and traces, a control map of tools and permissions, and rollback criteria
A statement that the model provider is reputable and widely used, which should reassure stakeholders about the agent's safety
The number of engineering hours spent building and refining the agent, as evidence of how carefully it was made

stem: An agent sometimes needs to ask the user a clarifying question; other times it should just answer. How should this behaviour be designed and tested?

choices.text: Instructions defining when ambiguity warrants one targeted clarification and when to proceed with an assumption, tested both ways
Always ask at least one clarifying question before answering anything, to be safe, even when the request is perfectly clear
Never ask clarifying questions; always guess the most likely intent and proceed, since users dislike being asked questions
Ask each user to configure a personal preference for how often the agent should ask clarifying questions before it answers

stem: An agent will be embedded in a module used by 20 teams with different data permissions. Which pre-release test specifically validates the permission behaviour?

choices.text: A load test with 20 concurrent users from one team, confirming that the agent stays responsive under the expected traffic
A single test run as an administrator who can see everything, confirming that the agent answers every question correctly
Asking the model directly in a conversation whether it respects user permissions and recording its answer as evidence
Running the same questions as users from several teams, asserting each sees only authorized data, including a no-access user
